title: The way of not-knowing
hookLine: Orthodox and mystics say what God is not, since God is beyond every idea

cards: The mountain is wrapped in smoke and cloud, and the ground shakes with thunder. The people at the bottom have had enough. They step back and want Moses to speak to them instead of God.
Then Exodus gives one quiet sentence: "And the people stood afar off, and Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was." Not into a blaze of light. Into the dark.
Some Christians have read that sentence as a map for prayer: the closer you come to God, the less you can see. Today's word: apophatic.

teach.b: Apophatic is usually explained from a Greek word for saying no. The apophatic way speaks of God by saying what God is not. Not a thing among other things.
Not made. Not in one place. Not limited.
Not the size of any idea we have. Each not clears away a picture that was too small. Its partner, the cataphatic way, says what God is: good, light, love.
Orthodox teaching holds the two together, and gives the not-saying a place of honor; mystics in the West walked the same road. The Bible keeps both in view.
God tells Moses, "Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live."
A letter to Timothy speaks of God "dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto; whom no man hath seen, nor can see." Light so bright it works like darkness.
Gregory of Nyssa, writing about the life of Moses, noticed the order of the story: Moses meets God first in light, at the burning bush, later in cloud, and at last in thick darkness.
For Gregory, going deeper meant seeing less, and knowing more.
In medieval England, an unknown writer made a small book of it, The Cloud of Unknowing. Its counsel, put simply: you won't reach God by thinking harder; reach into the cloud with love.
None of this is the same as knowing nothing. It keeps God larger than your best idea, and lets silence say what words can't.

how: Orthodox Christians speak of God both by what God is and, with special honor, by what God is not; in the West, contemplative Christians practice a similar wordless prayer, drawing on books like The Cloud of Unknowing.

o: a prayer said in total silence and darkness
speaking of God by saying what God is not
doubting whether God is there at all

games.q: the way of not-knowing — tap the pairs.
p: reach into the cloud with love

s: the apophatic way means believing nothing about God
it keeps God larger than any idea. Orthodox Christians hold it together with saying what God is.
in Exodus, Moses drew near to the thick darkness where God was
"and the people stood afar off, and Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was."
only the Eastern churches ever prayed this way
in medieval England an unknown writer made a book of it: The Cloud of Unknowing.

games.q: you're at the foot of Sinai. the mountain is wrapped in smoke and thick darkness, and the people are stepping back in fear. you're Moses. what do you do?
o: step back with the people and wait for it to clear.
draw near to the thick darkness where God is.
climb only once the cloud has lifted.
games.why: "Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was." Gregory of Nyssa read it as the deepest stage: going further in meant seeing less.

practice: Whatever you believe, try this as an exercise: on each out-breath, set down one picture of God that's too small. Not an old man on a cloud, not a vending machine, not my worst fear, not my best idea either.
When you run out, sit in the space that's left without filling it; if you pray, let that empty space be your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Apophatic. The way of not-knowing: speaking of God by saying what God is not, because God is beyond every idea.

orig.note: Greek: usually explained as a denial, a saying no; the root of apophatic.

carryVoice: Your line: more than you think. Silence can say it too. Same time tomorrow.
